entries.name: Cheniere — US LNG Export Anchor
entries.thesisShort: Cheniere is the largest US LNG exporter, with Corpus Christi Stage 3 more than 98% complete and full-year 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance raised for a second consecutive quarter to $7.9-8.4B.
entries.thesisLong:
Cheniere Energy is the largest US LNG exporter and the second-largest LNG operator globally, running Sabine Pass in Louisiana and Corpus Christi in Texas. The build phase that defined the last three years is now in its final mile: Trains 1 through 4 reached substantial completion in 2025, Trains 5 and 6 followed in March and June 2026, and FERC has cleared Cheniere to introduce gas into Train 7, the last of the seven midscale units, with substantial completion expected in the fall of 2026.

That completion is showing up in the numbers. Q2 2026 adjusted EBITDA was approximately $1.8 billion on a 20% year-over-year increase in exported LNG volumes, and Cheniere raised full-year 2026 guidance for the second consecutive quarter — adjusted EBITDA to $7.9-8.4 billion and distributable cash flow to $5.3-5.8 billion. Production guidance was tightened to 53-54 million tons as the Stage 3 ramp and improved facility reliability cut downtime.

The bottleneck is regulatory and capital intensity: a greenfield LNG terminal takes four to six years and $10-20 billion, which is why already-permitted brownfield expansion is the scarce asset. Cheniere is advancing the Sabine Pass Expansion under a roughly $4.7 billion EPC contract with Bechtel, with Phase I expected to add more than 6 million tons per annum and FID targeted within the next twelve to eighteen months.

The commercial model is largely take-or-pay at fixed fees plus a Henry Hub-linked variable, which insulates EBITDA from spot volatility while leaving uncontracted volumes exposed to European TTF and Asian JKM pricing. The risk sits at the other end of the decade: a potential global oversupply window as Qatari and remaining US capacity lands faster than demand absorbs it.

entries.name: Cheniere Energy Partners — Sabine Pass MLP
entries.thesisShort: CQP is the MLP that owns the Sabine Pass LNG terminal; it reconfirmed 2026 distribution guidance of $3.10-$3.40 per unit at Q2 2026 and declared $0.820 for the quarter.
entries.thesisLong:
Cheniere Energy Partners (CQP) is the publicly traded MLP that owns the Sabine Pass LNG terminal in Cameron Parish, Louisiana — the first US lower-48 facility to ship an LNG cargo (February 2016) and still one of the largest in the world. Cheniere Inc. is the general partner and majority holder; CQP exists to deliver predictable distributions to limited partners.

Q2 2026 delivered on that mandate. Net income rose to $1.16 billion, earnings beat on higher LNG margins, and management reconfirmed full-year 2026 distribution guidance of $3.10-$3.40 per common unit, with $3.10 as the base and the remainder variable on uncontracted margin. The Q2 2026 declared distribution was $0.820 per common unit — $0.775 base plus $0.045 variable — to unitholders of record on 7 August 2026.

The growth catalyst is the Sabine Pass Expansion, a brownfield addition adjacent to the existing terminal. Cheniere is advancing it under a roughly $4.7 billion EPC contract with Bechtel, with Phase I expected to add more than 6 million tons per annum and a final investment decision targeted within the next twelve to eighteen months. Brownfield expansion at an already-permitted site avoids the greenfield permitting risk that gates every new entrant.

Risks include MLP structure tax friction for some holders, a higher cost of equity than the C-corp parent, concentration in a single Gulf Coast site exposed to hurricane and grid risk, and margin compression on uncontracted volumes in a 2027-28 oversupply window.

entries.name: Marathon Petroleum — Coastal Refining Scale
entries.thesisShort: MPC operates the largest US refining footprint; its Q2 2026 refining and marketing margin doubled year over year to $36.33 per barrel with Gulf Coast refineries running flat out at 100%.
entries.thesisLong:
Marathon Petroleum operates the largest refining footprint in the United States, spanning the Gulf Coast (Galveston Bay, Garyville), Mid-Continent (Robinson, Detroit, Catlettsburg) and West Coast (Los Angeles, Anacortes, Martinez Renewables).

Q2 2026 was the quarter the West Coast supply story showed up in the P&L. Net income was $5.1 billion, or $17.73 per diluted share, against $1.2 billion and $3.96 a year earlier. The refining and marketing margin doubled to $36.33 per barrel from $17.58, driven by wider crack spreads across every region. The system ran at 94% of capacity on roughly 2.9 million barrels per day, with Gulf Coast refineries running flat out at 100%.

The structural driver is supply-side scarcity rather than demand strength. California refinery closures — Phillips 66's Wilmington shutdown in late 2025 and Valero's Benicia idle, completed in April 2026 — removed roughly 17% of West Coast capacity, and the region now leans harder on imports. That is a durable change to the PADD 5 supply curve rather than a cyclical swing.

MPC also owns the general partner and majority of MPLX, whose distribution stream funds a meaningful share of parent cash returns. Renewable diesel at Martinez and Dickinson adds a clean-fuels lane. The risks are demand-side and weather-side: gasoline plateauing as EV penetration rises, a recession compressing middle-distillate spreads, and hurricane disruption to the Galveston Bay complex.

entries.name: Phillips 66 — Mid-Cycle Refining Reset
entries.thesisShort: Phillips 66 ran 96% crude utilization in Q2 2026 as realized refining margins more than doubled sequentially to $24.08 per barrel, while Elliott continues to press for a midstream separation the company is resisting.
entries.thesisLong:
Phillips 66 shut its Wilmington refinery in Los Angeles (~139,000 bpd) in late 2025, removing a structurally challenged West Coast asset and concentrating throughput on its more profitable Gulf Coast and Mid-Continent system. Q2 2026 showed what that concentration is worth in a tight market: adjusted earnings of $9.41 per share, up 295% year over year, on adjusted earnings of $3.79 billion and net income of $3.8 billion. Worldwide realized refining margins jumped to $24.08 per barrel from $10.11 in Q1, with 96% crude utilization, 86% clean product yield and 98% market capture.

The governance question is now contested from inside the boardroom rather than from outside it. Elliott Management, holding 19.25 million shares worth roughly $3.25 billion, took its case to a proxy contest that ended in a split vote: of the four contested seats, Phillips 66 and Elliott each claimed two, giving Elliott a voice in board decisions without control of them. CEO Mark Lashier has publicly pushed back on the spin-off plan, arguing the midstream and refining businesses complement each other, and the company continues to grow midstream regardless. Readers tracking this entry should treat the separation as contested rather than pending — the campaign has a seat at the table, not a mandate.

The refining system spans facilities across the US and Europe, including Bayway, Sweeny, Lake Charles and Borger. The Rodeo Renewable Energy Complex gives PSX a position in low-carbon fuels, and the CPChem joint venture with Chevron plus Marketing & Specialties diversify away from pure refining beta.

Risks centre on the direction of the activist campaign, RIN and LCFS volatility hitting renewable diesel margins, European refining performance, and West Coast gasoline demand decline.

entries.name: Valero — Throughput King with Renewables Optionality
entries.thesisShort: Valero posted record Q2 2026 net income of $3.7B on a $23.62 per barrel refining margin, having completed the Benicia refinery idle in April 2026 and concentrated runs on higher-margin Gulf Coast assets.
entries.thesisLong:
Valero Energy is the most Gulf-Coast-concentrated of the US refining majors, anchored by Port Arthur, Texas City and St. Charles, and its cost structure per barrel is among the lowest in the peer set.

Q2 2026 was a record. Net income reached $3.7 billion with adjusted EPS of $12.54 and revenue of $44.48 billion. The Refining segment generated $4.47 billion of operating income against $1.266 billion a year earlier, on a refining margin of $6.342 billion — $23.62 per barrel — across 2.95 million barrels per day of throughput.

The Benicia idle is now history rather than plan: Valero completed the shutdown of refining operations at the Bay Area plant in April 2026. Combined with the Phillips 66 Wilmington closure, that removes roughly 17% of California in-state refining capacity, forcing greater reliance on imports and structurally tightening PADD 5. Valero exited an unprofitable geography while keeping marketing exposure to the higher prices that followed.

Diamond Green Diesel, the joint venture with Darling Ingredients, operates 1.2 billion gallons per year of renewable diesel capacity plus a 235 million gallon per year sustainable aviation fuel unit at Port Arthur. SAF demand from EU ReFuelEU mandates and US tax credits provides a long-duration second lane.

Risks include RIN and LCFS price weakness if California regulation softens, hurricane disruption given the Gulf Coast concentration, and recession compressing distillate cracks from an exceptional 1H 2026 base.

entries.name: Enbridge — Cross-Border Mainline Monopoly
entries.thesisShort: Enbridge's Mainline moves roughly 3 million bpd of Western Canadian crude to US refiners; the company reaffirmed 2026 guidance at Q2 and grew its secured capital backlog to C$41B.
entries.thesisLong:
Enbridge operates the largest crude oil pipeline system in North America. The Mainline transports approximately 3 million barrels per day of Western Canadian crude to US Midwest and Gulf Coast refiners, and with the Trans Mountain Expansion in service and filling, it remains the backbone of cross-border heavy oil flows.

Q2 2026 adjusted EBITDA was C$4,776 million against C$4,644 million a year earlier, with distributable cash flow of C$2,948 million, and management reaffirmed full-year 2026 guidance on the back of constructive rate cases and strong recontracting. The forward book is where the story has moved: the secured capital backlog grew to C$41 billion, the company secured up to C$20 billion of new projects for 2026-2027, and it frames roughly C$50 billion of organic growth opportunity through 2030.

The project list is diversifying the business away from the Canadian liquids core, and the Gulf Coast gas build is where it is concentrated. Blackcomb — the 2.5 bcf/d, roughly 365-mile Permian-to-Agua Dulce line owned 70% by the WPC joint venture alongside Targa at 17.5% and MPLX at 12.5% — is in commissioning, with start-up expected in October 2026 and volumes ramping through the second half. On 31 July 2026 the Whistler joint venture, in which Enbridge holds 19%, sanctioned Bay Runner Twin: up to 2.6 bcf/d from Agua Dulce to Rio Grande LNG under long-term take-or-pay agreements, in service by 2030. The Enbridge Houston Oil Terminal entered service, the roughly US$1 billion Wisconsin Line 5 relocation is under construction with service expected in early 2027, and Enbridge signed an exclusive option to acquire the TTC Connector, linking its Tres Palacios storage to Freeport LNG.

Risks are regulatory and macro: Line 5 continues to face tribal and state opposition, Western Canadian differentials widen if upstream supply outpaces takeaway, and higher long rates compress the multiple on a dividend-led equity.

entries.name: Enterprise Products — Permian-to-Coast NGL Toll Road
entries.thesisShort: Enterprise runs the largest US NGL system; Q2 2026 set a record $2.8B of EBITDA as the Neches River terminal's second phase entered service in May 2026 and lifted LPG exports by 141 MBPD.
entries.thesisLong:
Enterprise Products Partners is the largest US NGL pipeline and processing company, with an integrated system spanning Permian and Eagle Ford gathering, Mont Belvieu fractionation — the world's largest NGL hub — and Houston Ship Channel export terminals.

Q2 2026 set a record at $2.8 billion of EBITDA, driven by acute global demand for US energy through April and May that pulled volumes across crude, LPG and ethane channels. The Bahia Y-grade NGL pipeline, placed in service in Q4 2025, is now operating alongside Shin Oak at 86% of capacity — the system is filling rather than waiting for barrels.

Export capacity is the growth engine, it arrived early, and it filled immediately. The second phase of the Neches River ethane and propane terminal in Orange County, Texas was placed in service in May 2026, lifting LPG export volumes by 141 MBPD — and by mid-June the terminal was already moving 329 Mb/d of ethane against a 300 Mb/d nameplate, running above its rated capacity within weeks of start-up. The marine terminal expansion is commissioning ahead of its original schedule to meet international demand. That positions Enterprise to supply the ethane crackers in Asia and Europe that increasingly run on US-sourced feedstock.

The capital cycle has not turned down as cleanly as previously framed. 2026 gross capex is now $2.9-3.4 billion after asset sale proceeds with roughly $600 million of sustaining capex, and 2026 growth capex expectations have risen by more than $700 million since the start of the year, with 2027 growth capex near $3 billion. Harvest mode is being pushed out, not cancelled.

Risks include global petrochemical demand softness, MLP K-1 friction, ethane price weakness on US oversupply, and Houston Ship Channel weather disruption.

entries.name: Williams — Transco Gas Superhighway
entries.thesisShort: Williams' Transco is the largest-volume US natural gas pipeline, and the company raised 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance to $8.3-8.5B while lifting its long-term growth target to an 11%-plus CAGR through 2030.
entries.thesisLong:
Williams owns and operates Transco, the largest-volume natural gas pipeline in the United States, spanning more than 10,000 miles from South Texas to New York City. Transco is the spine connecting Gulf Coast LNG export demand, Northeast city-gate utility demand, and Marcellus and Haynesville production.

Q2 2026 adjusted EBITDA was $1.92 billion, up 6% year over year, with year-to-date EBITDA up 10%. Management raised full-year 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance by $200 million at the midpoint to $8.3-8.5 billion, from a prior $8.05-8.35 billion, and lifted the long-term EBITDA growth target to an 11%-plus compound annual rate through 2030 — a rare structural raise for a large-cap pipeline.

The growth is organic rather than acquired, which is the more important point for a bottleneck thesis. Williams already owns the right-of-way, so incremental capacity comes from compression and looping on an existing corridor rather than from siting a new line. Southeast Supply Enhancement is the clearest case: FERC's 29 January 2026 order authorised roughly 55 miles of new large-diameter pipe plus substantial compressor station upgrades, delivering up to 1.6 million dekatherms per day of incremental firm transportation into Southeast markets at an estimated $1.53 billion — and as of mid-2026 sections were tracking to enter service earlier than originally scheduled. Power Express would carry a further ~950 MMcf/d to markets north of Station 165 in Pittsylvania County, Virginia. That right-of-way is the asset that cannot be replicated, and it points directly at data center load in Virginia and the Carolinas alongside Gulf Coast LNG feedgas.

Risks include FERC tolling reform pressure on legacy Transco rates, Northeast pipeline siting opposition, execution on a multi-year expansion backlog, and Permian gas oversupply weighing on basis. The C-corp structure (no K-1) remains an advantage versus the MLP midstream names for institutional holders.

entries.name: SLB — International Offshore Reservoir Leader
entries.thesisShort: SLB is the global leader in high-end international and offshore services, but Q2 2026 showed the Middle East disruption biting: revenue of $8.97B grew sequentially even as international revenue fell 6% year over year.
entries.thesisLong:
SLB is the global leader in oilfield services, with roughly 30% of the high-end international and offshore drilling and reservoir technology market — about double its nearest competitor. Its dominance in subsurface complexity makes it the preferred partner for national oil companies including Saudi Aramco, Petrobras, ADNOC and Equinor.

Q2 2026 is where the thesis and the tape diverged. Revenue of $8.97 billion rose 3% sequentially and 5% year over year, with EPS of $0.52, and sequential growth was broad-based across North America, Latin America, Europe and Africa, and Asia. But that growth had to more than offset a 13% sequential revenue decline in the Middle East caused by persistent conflict-related disruption. On a year-over-year basis, international revenue fell 6% and North American revenue fell 1%.

The structural case is unchanged and still ahead: deepwater activity in Brazil's pre-salt, Guyana's Stabroek Block, Suriname's Block 58 and Namibia's Orange Basin is at multi-decade highs, and SLB's subsea, reservoir and digital technology command the highest premiums on exactly those complex projects. The ChampionX acquisition and the Delfi digital platform further diversify away from pure rig-count beta.

The honest read on 2026 is that the Middle East disruption is not a rounding error — it is the single largest swing factor in the near-term numbers, and it is geopolitical rather than commercial, which makes it hard to underwrite either direction. The mechanism is specific: a force majeure declaration in Qatar, production shut-ins in Iraq, and security-driven demobilization of offshore operations across the region. A gradual recovery is now unfolding — activity has been restored and is strengthening in the UAE and Qatar, and national oil companies are seeking solutions deployable at scale to bring back wells shuttered during the conflict — but mid-August 2026 brought stalled ceasefire talks and renewed Strait of Hormuz concerns, so the recovery is directional rather than secured. Brazil and Namibia FID timing and the pace of the OPEC+ unwind are the other variables.

entries.name: Halliburton — North American Completions Powerhouse
entries.thesisShort: Halliburton is the largest North American completions provider with roughly 40% of pressure pumping; Q2 2026 revenue rose 4% to $5.7B as international growth offset conflict-driven Middle East and Asia declines.
entries.thesisLong:
Halliburton is the largest North American completions services provider, with roughly 40% market share in pressure pumping and leading positions in cementing, wireline and artificial lift. Its US land concentration has historically made it the highest-beta major services name to Permian and Lower 48 activity.

Q2 2026 revenue was $5.7 billion, up 4% year over year, with operating income of $778 million. The shape of the growth is the notable part: international revenue rose 6% year to date and carried the quarter, offsetting declines in the Middle East and Asia tied to the same geopolitical conflict that hit SLB. For a company whose bear case has always been North American concentration, an internationally led quarter is a meaningful change in the mix.

The technology lever is the Zeus electric frac platform, which replaces diesel engines with grid-tied or gas-fuelled electric pumps, lowering customer fuel cost and emissions while commanding premium pricing. Zeus is the conversion path for the US frac fleet and the main reason Halliburton can hold pricing when rig counts do not grow.

Service intensity per well continues to rise — longer laterals, more proppant per foot — which partially decouples revenue from rig count. The risks are the mirror image: pricing concessions from Tier 1 customers if activity softens, continued Middle East disruption, and electric fleet conversion cannibalizing legacy diesel margins during the transition.

entries.name: Baker Hughes — LNG Turbomachinery & Industrial Tech
entries.thesisShort: Baker Hughes' Industrial & Energy Technology segment supplies the turbomachinery at the heart of LNG liquefaction; record Q2 2026 IET orders of $7.1B doubled year over year at a 2.2x book-to-bill.
entries.thesisLong:
Baker Hughes runs two distinct businesses: Oilfield Services & Equipment (OFSE) and Industrial & Energy Technology (IET), the turbomachinery, compressor and emissions franchise inherited from GE Oil & Gas. IET is what makes Baker Hughes structurally different from SLB and Halliburton — it supplies the aeroderivative gas turbines and centrifugal compressors that sit at the heart of LNG liquefaction trains.

Q2 2026 was a record on the order line. Total orders reached $10.5 billion, up 49% year over year, with IET orders of $7.1 billion — double the prior year — at a 2.2x book-to-bill that lifted remaining performance obligations 19% to $37.1 billion. LNG equipment orders alone were $1.8 billion across three large projects, including liquefaction equipment for Cheniere's Sabine Pass Train 7 awarded through Bechtel, plus a boil-off gas re-liquefaction unit and fleet-wide gas turbine upgrades. A Venture Global award added six LNG blocks — twelve liquefaction modules, each built around two single mixed-refrigerant units and their compression trains, using Baker Hughes centrifugal compressor technology.

The second leg is newer and is why this entry is no longer purely an LNG story. Power Systems orders totalled $2.6 billion including 2.7 gigawatts of power generation, and management is targeting Horizon 2 IET orders above $45 billion — the same data center and grid demand that shows up in the GE Vernova and Eaton entries, arriving through a different supplier.

OFSE revenue was $3.45 billion, up 7% sequentially, on total quarterly revenue of $6.7 billion, with 2026 revenue forecast around $27.35 billion. The all-cash Chart Industries acquisition has closed, and integration is now being measured against a $325 million cost synergy target and a stated aim of returning net debt to adjusted EBITDA to 1.0-1.5x within twenty-four months of closing. The backlog provides good visibility into 2027. Risks remain LNG project deferrals, IET margin volatility from lumpy order timing, and competition from Mitsubishi Heavy Industries and Siemens Energy in turbomachinery.

entries.name: Diamondback Energy — Permian Pure-Play Champion
entries.thesisShort: Diamondback is the largest pure-play Permian operator and crossed one million BOE per day for the first time in Q2 2026, raising full-year oil guidance to 522+ MBO/d while holding capex at about $3.9 billion.
entries.thesisLong:
Diamondback closed the $26 billion Endeavor Energy Resources acquisition in late 2024, doubling its Permian inventory and creating the largest pure-play operator in the basin.

Q2 2026 was a milestone quarter. Oil production averaged 525 MBO/d, at the top of guidance, and total production of 1,018 MBOE/d pushed average output above one million BOE per day for the first time in company history. Management raised full-year guidance to 522-plus MBO/d and 1,000-plus MBOE/d while holding the cash capital budget at approximately $3.9 billion — the combination that matters most in this business, since production upside without capex upside is what free cash flow is made of.

The cash generation followed. Q2 net cash from operating activities was $3.6 billion with $2.3 billion of free cash flow, and per-share net cash from operations, free cash flow and oil production grew 49%, 81% and 21% respectively against Q2 2024. Q3 2026 cash capex is guided to $950-1,050 million.

Capital return discipline remains the core of the equity story: a base-plus-variable dividend, with the variable portion scaling to oil prices, complemented by buybacks. Diamondback's break-even sits near the bottom of the US E&P cohort, which is what allows the variable component to survive a soft strip.

The gas side of the basin has been the swing variable, and it has moved. Q2 2026 gas realizations were pressured to -$2.15 per Mcf by Permian takeaway constraints, with Waha approaching -$10 per Mcf during maintenance — but the basis turned positive in July as new takeaway capacity began coming online, and Waha cash traded around $2.10 on 14 August 2026 in a $1.80-$2.23 weekly range. The pipeline build that shows up in the Enbridge entry is what relieved it, which is the sort of cross-layer dependency this section exists to make visible.

Risks include Permian inventory quality degradation over time, sustained low oil prices pressuring the variable dividend, renewed Waha volatility around maintenance windows, and regulatory friction on water disposal and flaring.

entries.name: EOG Resources — Multi-Basin Execution Leader
entries.thesisShort: EOG has become a genuine multi-basin operator, and in Q2 2026 it beat its $150 million Encino synergy target ahead of schedule while cutting Utica direct well costs 20% to below $600 per foot.
entries.thesisLong:
EOG Resources is the most operationally efficient large-cap US E&P, known for premium-only drilling and top-quartile capital efficiency. The $5.6 billion Encino Acquisition Partners deal elevated the Utica Shale in Ohio to a foundational play alongside the Delaware Basin and Eagle Ford, adding substantial gas exposure as LNG and data center power demand accelerate.

Q2 2026 was a record and the integration is the reason. EOG delivered adjusted EPS of $5.70, adjusted cash flow from operations per share of $8.29, and $2.8 billion of free cash flow, on net cash from operations of $4.67 billion against capital expenditures of $1.587 billion. Net income was $2,724 million on revenue of $8,620 million. Production reached 548.8 MBo/d of oil and 1,410.4 MBoed total, with cash operating costs of $10.57 per Boe.

The Utica numbers are what validate the acquisition thesis rather than merely restating it. EOG exceeded its $150 million Encino synergy target ahead of schedule, cut direct well costs below $600 per foot — down 20% from where Encino left them — lifted drilling and completion speeds by double digits, and more than tripled activity levels versus pre-acquisition rates. That is the operating-system transfer the deal was underwritten on, showing up within four quarters.

Shareholder returns held: $1.8 billion in the quarter, comprising $540 million of regular dividends and $1.29 billion of share repurchases.

Risks include Appalachian gas oversupply weighing on Utica realizations, execution complexity managing three foundational basins simultaneously, and sustained weakness in oil prices.

entries.name: Centrus Energy — HALEU Fuel Cycle Monopoly
entries.thesisShort: Centrus is the only US producer of High-Assay Low-Enriched Uranium, and it has now converted the $900M DOE award into a commercial build — total backlog reached $4.5B extending to 2040, with a definitive X-energy supply contract signed in August 2026.
entries.thesisLong:
Centrus Energy operates the only US-licensed cascade producing High-Assay Low-Enriched Uranium (HALEU) — the 5-20% U-235 fuel required by the next generation of advanced reactors, including TerraPower Natrium, X-energy Xe-100, Kairos KP-FHR, Oklo Aurora and BWXT TRISO microreactors. The American Centrifuge Plant in Piketon, Ohio produced the nation's first HALEU under DOE contract.

The $900 million DOE HALEU enrichment award, signed in mid-2026, has since moved from award to execution. It carries options exercisable at DOE's discretion for up to an additional $170 million of HALEU production and delivery, and Centrus entered an EPC contract with Fluor in February 2026 for the commercial expansion and deployment of both LEU and HALEU production capability at Piketon, with commercial production expected to commence in 2029.

The order book is the clearest evidence the commercial phase is real. Total backlog reached $4.5 billion at 30 June 2026, up roughly $600 million in the quarter and now extending to 2040. Of that, the LEU segment carries about $3.7 billion — including $3.0 billion of contingent LEU and HALEU commitments supporting potential construction at Piketon, of which $2.4 billion sits under definitive agreements — with Technical Solutions holding the remaining $0.8 billion. On 6 August 2026 the first-of-a-kind commercial agreement took definitive form: Centrus signed a contract to supply X-energy with LEU and HALEU enrichment services, with deliveries from the American Centrifuge Plant beginning in 2030. Nearly two metric tons of HALEU UF6 have been produced for the government under the current operations contract.

The counterweight sits in the other segment. The FY 2027 DOE budget proposal does not include further funding for operating the HALEU cascade under the Technical Solutions contract — the government programme that produced the nation's first HALEU is not assured of continued funding even as the commercial book grows.

The operational tells point the same direction. Piketon hiring guidance was raised to more than 175 net new employees for the full year, up from a prior goal of 100, and the first new centrifuge at Oak Ridge, Tennessee is expected to be complete by year-end 2026. Q2 2026 revenue was $176.1 million against $154.5 million a year earlier, with GAAP net income of $16.8 million and non-GAAP adjusted net income of $38.7 million.

Beyond HALEU, Centrus is the largest US-based supplier of Low-Enriched Uranium for existing light-water reactors. The Russia uranium ban phases out US imports of Russian enriched uranium, which historically supplied roughly 20% of US needs through TENEX — a forced re-shoring that creates a multi-decade Western enrichment shortage.

Where this differs from the nuclear utility plays: Centrus is the bottleneck at the enrichment step. Without HALEU, no advanced reactor design reaches commercial operation. Risks remain heavy — dependence on DOE contract options, advanced reactor timelines slipping, Urenco USA HALEU plans, and the capital required for commercial-scale expansion.

entries.name: First Solar — US Module Manufacturing Monopoly
entries.thesisShort: First Solar is the only US-headquartered solar module manufacturer at scale, running a roughly 57% gross margin in Q2 2026 on a 45.1 GW contracted backlog — though the backlog has drawn down from 50.1 GW at year-end 2025.
entries.thesisLong:
First Solar is the largest US-headquartered solar module manufacturer and the only major Tier 1 player using cadmium telluride thin-film rather than silicon, with domestic capacity across Ohio, Alabama and Louisiana and a sixth US facility — a finishing plant in South Carolina — expected in the second half of 2026.

Q2 2026 was profitable and orderly: net sales of approximately $1.06 billion, net income up 24% to $423 million, and gross margin expanding to about 57%. The company surpassed 100 gigawatts of cumulative module sales and reaffirmed full-year 2026 net sales guidance of $4.9-5.2 billion.

The backlog is the number to watch, and it is going the wrong way. Contracted backlog stood at 45.1 GW worth roughly $13.6 billion as of 30 June 2026, down from 50.1 GW at year-end 2025: First Solar sold 7.6 GW in the period but booked only 2.8 GW of new orders, with minimal de-bookings. A manufacturer shipping faster than it books is drawing down its forward visibility, and that is the honest counterweight to a 57% gross margin. The remaining backlog does extend through 2030, and 41 of the 45.1 GW carry at least some domestic content requirement.

The reason for the booking slowdown is identifiable rather than mysterious, which matters for reading it. Management attributes it to customers delaying decisions pending clarity on Section 232 tariff policy — a decision that could land in August, September or later. That makes the drawdown a timing question tied to a specific pending ruling rather than evidence of lost competitive position, though a slip pushes the resolution further out.

One policy mechanic changed materially. Q2 2026 included no Section 45X tax credit discounts, reflecting a management decision not to sell tax credits in 2026 — so the tax-credit-transfer monetization route that previously converted 45X into near-term cash is not being used this year. The quarter did include an $89 million tariff recovery under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, while higher non-recoverable domestic freight costs are expected to pressure second-half margins.

The bottleneck thesis remains policy-locked: domestic content adders and 45X credits create a cost position Chinese imports cannot match while the subsidies stand. Risks are the flip side — 45X repeal or modification, overseas facility underutilization, tariff whiplash, and utility-scale project cancellations.

entries.name: Enphase Energy — Microinverter Cycle Recovery
entries.thesisShort: Enphase leads the US residential microinverter market, but the Section 25D residential credit has expired and US sell-through fell 34% year over year — Q2 2026 growth came from Europe, where revenue rose about 35%.
entries.thesisLong:
Enphase Energy is the dominant US residential solar microinverter manufacturer, sharing a duopoly with SolarEdge. Its microinverter architecture — one inverter per panel — is preferred for safety, reliability and module-level monitoring versus the optimizer-plus-string approach.

The policy backdrop has changed decisively, and it is the single most important fact in this entry. The Section 25D residential clean energy credit — worth 30% of installation cost — expired on 31 December 2025 under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. US residential sell-through was down 34% year over year in Q2 2026 under the combination of high interest rates and that expiration, and SEIA with Wood Mackenzie forecast an 18% drop in US residential installations for 2026, with Enphase itself guiding to roughly a 22% decline and Sunrun to 25%. The prior framing of this entry — a cyclical trough with the IRA underwriting recovery — no longer holds: the subsidy that underwrote residential demand is gone.

What is working is geographic. Q2 2026 revenue was $291.9 million, up 3% sequentially, with US revenue down roughly 3% sequentially and European revenue up about 35%. The company shipped 1.59 million microinverters and 113.8 megawatt-hours of batteries and generated $25.9 million of free cash flow — profitable through the downturn, but growing outside its home market.

The storage attach rate remains the structural offset. Time-of-use rate proliferation and grid reliability concerns push residential customers toward solar-plus-storage economics that do not depend on a federal credit, and battery megawatt-hours are the line where that shows up.

Risks are substantial: further US residential contraction post-25D, competition from Tesla's integrated ecosystem, lower-cost Chinese inverter brands entering via channel partners, and tariff pressure on margins.

entries.name: SolarEdge — Post-Subsidy Manufacturing Pivot
entries.thesisShort: SolarEdge returned to non-GAAP operating profit in Q2 2026 for the first time in nearly three years, on $346M of revenue and a Nexis ramp that exceeded $60M of three-phase shipments in Europe.
entries.thesisLong:
SolarEdge is the second pillar of the residential inverter duopoly, pairing string inverters with module-level power optimizers. The company entered a deep crisis across 2024-2025 on European inventory destocking, residential rate pressure and a since-divested e-mobility misstep.

Q2 2026 is the first quarter that substantiates the turnaround rather than describing it. Revenue was $346 million, up 20% year over year, non-GAAP gross margin expanded to 28.6%, and the company posted non-GAAP operating income of $10.2 million — its first non-GAAP operating profit in nearly three years. For a company whose entire bear case was cash burn, crossing back into operating profitability is the milestone that matters.

Nexis, the next-generation inverter family, is carrying it. Three-phase Nexis shipments exceeded $60 million in Europe during the quarter, and retrofit upsell activity generated more than $20 million, driven by homeowner demand for storage additions in the Netherlands and the DACH region. A US volume rollout is planned for the second half of 2026, supported by approvals across major financing platforms including TPO and prepaid PPA products — which matters more than usual now that the US residential market has lost the Section 25D credit, which expired on 31 December 2025 and third-party ownership structures carry more of the demand.

Guidance tempers the enthusiasm. Q3 2026 revenue is guided to $310-340 million with non-GAAP gross margin of 22-26% and operating expenses of $86-91 million — a sequential step down at both the revenue and margin line, with management noting the range excludes any significant pull-forward.

Risks remain execution-shaped: US Nexis adoption against Enphase, Tesla ecosystem displacement, and sustaining profitability through a guided-down quarter.

entries.name: Peabody Energy — Met Coal via Centurion
entries.thesisShort: Peabody is pivoting to Australian metallurgical coal via Centurion, where the longwall issues that hit Q2 2026 have largely been resolved — but the 2026 sales target is now 2.5 Mt with the next longwall move pushed into early 2027.
entries.thesisLong:
Peabody Energy is the largest US coal producer by revenue, with operations in the Powder River Basin, Illinois Basin and Australia. The strategy is a decisive pivot away from secularly declining US thermal coal toward seaborne metallurgical coal via the Centurion mine, an Australian premium hard coking coal asset.

Q2 2026 shows the cost of executing that pivot mid-stream. Revenue rose to $1,003.2 million from $890.1 million a year earlier, but Peabody reported a net loss attributable to common stockholders of $90.6 million, or $0.74 per diluted share, against a $27.6 million loss a year earlier. Adjusted EBITDA fell to $24 million from $93.3 million. The seaborne thermal segment carried the quarter with more than $52 million of adjusted EBITDA at a 23% margin on 3.0 million tons shipped at $52-57 per ton of cost.

Centurion remains the swing factor and it is not resolved. The picture improved materially over the summer. At an 11 August 2026 investor tour of the mine, Peabody said the shield racking caused by the slow start and roof-control issues is fully addressed, with production increasing through July and early August and operations on pace for third-quarter targets; the remaining roof-control work is limited to a rock faulting zone spanning about 20% of the longwall face. The trade-off is schedule: the 2026 Centurion sales target is now 2.5 million tons, and the next longwall move has shifted into early 2027. Seaborne metallurgical shipments of 1.9-2.1 million tons carry costs of $130-140 per ton. Management expects a stronger second half as Centurion ramps and US thermal volumes recover — which is the same expectation that has been deferred through several quarters.

The demand-side case is intact. Pricing has softened, though. Premium hard coking coal assessed around $214.90 per wet metric tonne FOB Australia on 7 August 2026, about 10% below the 10 July level, after a July that averaged $233.08 in a $226-242 range. Chinese steelmakers account for roughly 45% of premium HCC spot transactions, so the benchmark is set largely by a single buyer bloc. Indian and Southeast Asian steel demand is the growth vector; Chinese demand is the volatility.

One further development belongs in the record: a securities class action has been filed against Peabody alleging investor harm in connection with Centurion, with a lead plaintiff deadline in late August 2026. The litigation is at its earliest stage and no findings have been made.

entries.name: NextEra Energy — Utility + Renewables Platform
entries.thesisShort: NextEra pairs Florida Power & Light with the largest US renewables developer, holds a record 35.1 GW Energy Resources backlog, and in May 2026 agreed an all-stock combination with Dominion Energy valued at roughly $67 billion.
entries.thesisLong:
NextEra Energy is the parent of two complementary platforms: Florida Power & Light, the largest US regulated electric utility by retail sales, and NextEra Energy Resources, the largest developer of wind, solar and battery storage in North America.

The defining 2026 development is structural rather than operational. On 18 May 2026, NextEra and Dominion Energy agreed to combine in an all-stock transaction, with Dominion shareholders receiving 0.8138 NextEra shares per Dominion share, leaving NextEra and Dominion holders with roughly 74.5% and 25.5% of the combined company. The deal values Dominion at approximately $66.8 billion and would create a combined enterprise of roughly $420 billion — described by both companies as the world's largest regulated electric utility business. Regulatory applications were filed on 15 July 2026 with the Virginia SCC, the North Carolina Utilities Commission, the South Carolina PSC, FERC and the NRC, accompanied by a proposal for $2.25 billion of aggregate customer rate credits allocated by usage and payable over the two years following closing. The procedural calendar is now set: South Carolina intervention closes on 10 September 2026, Virginia evidentiary hearings begin on 17 November 2026, the South Carolina hearing follows on 8 December 2026 against a 29 January 2027 final order deadline, and the parties expect to close in the second half of 2027. Everything else in this entry is subject to that process.

The underlying businesses continue to compound. Q2 2026 adjusted earnings were $1.15 per share, and the Energy Resources backlog reached a record 35.1 gigawatts after adding 3.6 GW during the quarter, including 2 GW of battery storage. The standalone and co-located storage pipeline exceeds 110 gigawatts.

Florida is where the AI demand lands. FPL raised its large-load expectation to 8 gigawatts by 2032, up from 6 gigawatts, with 21 gigawatts of interest on the table and 12 gigawatts in advanced talks. FPL net income rose 11% to $1.41 billion and the utility added more than 90,000 customers in the quarter.

Risks now include merger approval and integration risk across five regulators, alongside federal subsidy modification affecting Energy Resources economics, rate sensitivity in a dividend-led equity, and Florida hurricane exposure.

entries.name: Eaton — Electrical Equipment Bottleneck
entries.thesisShort: Eaton sits at the tightest point in the grid build: total electrical backlog rose 43% year over year in Q2 2026, against transformer lead times of roughly 128 weeks and specialized high-voltage orders stretching toward four years.
entries.thesisLong:
Eaton is one of the most direct industrial beneficiaries of electrification, and the constraint it sits on is physical rather than commercial.

Q2 2026 quantified the demand. Total electrical backlog was up 43% year over year, total company backlog at the end of June was up 33% against June 2025, and the twelve-month rolling average of Electrical Americas orders rose 41% organically. Data center organic revenue grew 65% against an underlying market rate of about 23%, and data center orders rose roughly 240% year over year. Eaton raised organic growth guidance alongside the print.

The acute bottleneck is transformers. Wood Mackenzie’s transformer supply survey puts power transformer lead times at roughly 128 weeks and generator step-up units at about 144 weeks — near two and a half years — with some specialized orders extending to four. The same work models a national supply deficit of about 30% for power transformers, narrowing below 10% only by 2030, against demand growth since 2019 of 274% for GSUs and 116% for substation power transformers. The root cause is upstream of the transformer builders: Cleveland-Cliffs is the sole domestic producer of the grain-oriented electrical steel every transformer core requires, only ten to twelve manufacturers worldwide make high-grade GOES, and GOES prices have risen nearly 100% since January 2020. Switchgear is similarly constrained.

Eaton is adding capacity against it, including a $340 million three-phase transformer facility in Jonesville, South Carolina, with production and hiring beginning in 2027. That timing is the point: even a committed capacity response arrives years after the order.

This entry deliberately overlaps with the AI sector's power infrastructure layer. The angle here is the broader grid bottleneck affecting every energy capacity addition — utility-scale solar and wind, transmission upgrades, industrial electrification — not only AI data centers. The announced US data center pipeline of 307 gigawatts is roughly fifteen years of construction at the 2025 build rate, and most of Eaton's data center backlog delivers in 2028 and beyond.

Risks include order normalization after the 2025-26 surge, copper and steel cost inflation, and competition from Hitachi Energy, Siemens Energy and GE Vernova.
